extraction.name: PIQA (Physical Interaction: Question Answering)
extraction.description: PIQA is a benchmark dataset for evaluating physical commonsense reasoning in natural language understanding models. Given a physical goal expressed in natural language, a model must choose the most sensible solution from two options. The dataset focuses on everyday situations with a preference for atypical solutions, inspired by instructables.com. It contains over 16,000 training QA pairs, 2K development, and 3K test pairs. Humans achieve 95% accuracy while large pretrained models like RoBERTa achieve ~77%.
extraction.creator: Yonatan Bisk, Rowan Zellers, Ronan Le Bras, Jianfeng Gao, Yejin Choi
extraction.publisher: Allen Institute for Artificial Intelligence; Microsoft Research AI; Carnegie Mellon University; Paul G. Allen School for Computer Science and Engineering, University of Washington
extraction.citeAs: Bisk, Y., Zellers, R., Le Bras, R., Gao, J., & Choi, Y. (2020). PIQA: Reasoning about Physical Commonsense in Natural Language. AAAI.
extraction.rai:dataCollection: Data was collected via crowdsourcing using instructables.com as a scaffold. Annotators were provided links to instructables (drawn from six categories: costume, outside, craft, home, food, and workshop) to inspire them to construct goal-solution pairs. Annotators articulated a physical goal, a valid solution, and a 'trick' (an incorrect solution that sounds reasonable but is wrong due to subtle misunderstanding of preconditions or physics). Two examples were drawn per instructable. A qualification HIT was used where annotators had to identify well-formed (goal, solution) pairs with >80% accuracy to participate. Data was collected in batches and validated by other annotators for correctness.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionRawData: Instructables from instructables.com, a crowdsourced collection of instructions for activities from cooking to car repair, used as inspiration/prompts for annotators across six categories: costume, outside, craft, home, food, and workshop.
extraction.rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: The AFLite algorithm was applied to remove stylistic artifacts and trivial examples. 5,000 examples from the original dataset were used to fine-tune BERT-Large, then embeddings were computed for remaining instances. AFLite uses an ensemble of linear classifiers trained on random subsets to determine whether pre-computed embeddings are strong indicators of the correct answer option, and discards such instances. The train, development, and test folds were automatically produced by AFLite.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Annotators were shown an instructable to inspire them, and asked to: (1) articulate a physical goal, (2) provide a valid solution, and (3) provide a 'trick' - a permutation of their own solution which makes it invalid, often subtly. A 'diff' button highlighted where solutions differ to help annotators. Examples with low agreement during validation were removed. A qualification HIT was required before main annotation, with annotators needing >80% accuracy identifying well-formed pairs. Data was validated by other annotators for correctness; users with low agreement were de-qualified.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationPlatform: Amazon Mechanical Turk (implied by HIT terminology and turkerview.com reference)
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: Examples with low agreement during validation were removed, which sometimes meant that correct examples requiring expert-level domain knowledge were removed to keep the dataset focused on commonsense. Human performance was calculated by majority vote, using annotators who achieved >90% on the qualification HIT.
extraction.rai:machineAnnotationTools: Spacy (for tokenization and POS tagging); GPT BPE tokenizer; BERT-Large (used within AFLite for embeddings)
extraction.rai:dataSocialImpact: The authors aim to elicit research into building language representations that capture details of the real world, to enable language models useful beyond the NLP community, including for bootstrapping robotic-language applications. They argue knowledge should ultimately be learned from interaction with the world.
extraction.rai:dataBiases: The paper acknowledges reporting bias as a key issue in physical commonsense - commonsense properties are rarely directly reported in text. The authors specifically designed their collection methodology (using instructables as inspiration) to flatten the distribution of referenced objects and counter annotators' tendency to default to prototypical solutions (e.g., kitchen/garage tools). AFLite was used to remove stylistic artifacts and annotation biases that might artificially inflate model performance.
extraction.rai:dataLimitations: The dataset focuses on physical commonsense expressed in language, but the authors argue that true physical knowledge should be learned from interaction with the world. Some 'mistakes' identified in evaluation actually required web-search to verify. Examples were truncated at 150 tokens, affecting ~1% of the data. The dataset is in English only.
extraction.rai:dataUseCases: Training, validation, and testing of natural language understanding models on physical commonsense reasoning. The dataset serves as a benchmark for evaluating physical commonsense understanding and as a diagnostic for probing physical knowledge in pretrained language models.
